source.title: ProtSAE: Disentangling and Interpreting Protein Language Models via Semantically-Guided Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Xiang-Yu Liu; H. Lei; Yi Liu; Yang Liu; Wei Hu

record.file_problem: The paper is present in full. Some figure content is garbled and some table text is flattened; the relevance results in Figure 4a are described in the text but their exact values are not recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares semantic alignment of SAE features using relevance scores, a different measurement aimed at semantic disentanglement. It tests whether training changes affect feature alignment, but does not count polysemantic neurons directly.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is the comparison of relevance-based feature interpretation in Figure 4a. The paper also reports probing and reconstruction results, but these evaluate protein-function prediction and reconstruction fidelity rather than directly measuring neuron polysemanticity; they are not included as rows. The authors' statements that ProtSAE improves disentanglement are supported qualitatively, while exact Figure 4a values are unavailable in the text.
record.test_reason: The study builds a supervised SAE (ProtSAE) for ESM2-15B and compares its concept-relevance F1 with Naive, Gated and TopK SAEs. These are dictionary features of an SAE, not neurons of the network, and ProtSAE's alignment is induced by training on annotation labels. The paper cites neuron or feature entanglement as motivation (Joshi et al. 2025) but reports no rate or degree of polysemanticity in the model's own neurons. Its results are its own method's performance against baselines, so it is T4, not a test of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that semantically guided training (annotation guidance plus ontology axioms, forced activation and rescaling) yields SAE features more aligned with biological concepts than standard SAEs. They add that it keeps comparable reconstruction fidelity, gives better probing results and enables concept steering. The claim concerns SAE features in ESM2, not the PLM's raw neurons.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a semantically guided TopK SAE using protein annotations, ontology constraints, forced activations, and feature rescaling. It does not reproduce the original circuits or SoLU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Relevance F1 is evaluated after selecting the activation threshold that maximizes F1 from a stated set of thresholds. The study does not report a comparison of outcomes across threshold choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervising SAE latents with annotation and ontology losses gives SAE features with higher concept-relevance F1 than unsupervised SAEs on ESM2-15B. Reconstruction fidelity stays comparable (Loss Recovered roughly 0.68–0.99 across settings, similar to baselines).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept entanglement of SAE dictionary features (not model neurons) depends on the SAE's training objective and can be reduced with supervision at little reconstruction cost.

record.problems: The relevance results are shown in a figure with values not recoverable from the supplied text; no uncertainty estimates are stated. The paper evaluates only ESM2-15B and a limited set of concepts for relevance interpretation. Relevance F1 is an indirect measure of semantic alignment, not a count of polysemantic neurons.
record.rows_left_out: Protein-function probing, reconstruction-fidelity, and steering results were not extracted as rows because they do not directly measure neuron polysemanticity or feature-concept relevance. Their qualitative role is noted in gate_note and authors_conclusion.

untested.parts: No count of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models, and no comparison by layer. Only layer 35 of ESM2-15B is used, as SAE input.
Superposition is assumed as the basis for SAEs, not tested.
The network's own neurons are never measured. The SAE variants compared are interpretation tools, not changes to the network's activation function, architecture or training.
Not addressed. Fig. 4b shows top-activated features relating to nearby concepts (e.g. vacuole types), but this is about SAE features, not canonical neurons.
The F1 threshold is chosen to maximise F1 from a fixed set. No sensitivity to this choice is reported.

record.verdict_notes: The reader marked this as a T2 test of V5. That is not right. The paper concerns SAE dictionary features, and ProtSAE's monosemanticity is imposed by supervised labels, which falls under the exclusions for induced behaviour and for mitigation methods. No neuron-level polysemanticity rate for ESM2 is reported. All rows are comparisons of the authors' own method against baselines, and the Fig. 4a values cannot be read from the text.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses protein language models, not image classifiers or vision neurons.
It does not measure how often MLP neurons in transformer language models respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, or compare such rates by layer.
The paper invokes linear feature superposition as a basis for SAE, but does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
The study does not test polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is sufficient capacity.

It compares SAE training methods on ESM2-15B, but does not test SoLU, modern convnets, other model architectures, or the proportion of all neurons that are polysemantic. Its relevance measure assesses feature-concept alignment rather than directly counting polysemantic neurons.
It does not investigate whether canonical mixed features detect a shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
The study selects an activation threshold to maximize F1 but does not compare conclusions across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.
